 Oct 22, 2026 

 By Arvind Gopalakrishnan, Eugene Rakhmatulin, Manini Sharma and Prerit Rodney 

 AI-Generated Summary 

- NVIDIA DGX Spark now supports official eight-node clusters, scaling unified memory to 1 TB and enabling local execution of frontier-class models such as the full GLM 5.3 (753B) from Z.ai.
- A Spark-optimized collective backend called RoCEnante reduces all-reduce latency for tensor-parallel decode on switch-connected clusters, delivering a 4.43x decode speedup at eight nodes compared to 3.05x without it.
- Benchmark data shows decode throughput scaling from roughly 12 tokens per second on one node to 52 tokens per second on eight nodes using Qwen3.8-27B (NVFP4), with switch topologies enabling flexible workload partitioning and ring topologies offering cost-effective four-node inference.
- NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard routes requests between model pools on a shared eight-node cluster, matching Qwen-only quality on a tool-use benchmark while raising aggregate throughput up to 3x when most traffic shifts to a smaller model.
- Pre-training a nanochat model from scratch across eight nodes achieves a 7.79x speedup at 97.4% scaling efficiency, demonstrating near-linear training performance for small models on the desk.

...

AI developers aren’t just running a single model anymore—they’re orchestrating multiple models in parallel, chaining inference calls, and experimenting with frontier-class architectures that demand hundreds of gigabytes of memory. NVIDIA DGX Spark was built to bring AI development to the desk, and now you’ll be able to link even more Spark nodes together.

## Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) have transformed knowledge discovery, but their use in sensitive domains is limited by privacy concerns and risks of data leakage. Moreover, LLMs may hallucinate when queried about information outside their training data, undermining their reliability for scientific, clinical, or policy-related tasks. We present MyGPT, a fully open-source, privacy-preserving retrieval-augmented-generation (RAG) platform that uses open-source LLMs and operates locally or within secure institutional environments. MyGPT empowers users to query user-defined libraries such as biomedical literature, confidential clinical documents, and multilingual global health policies, while ensuring that sensitive data never leaves the secure environment. We introduce confidence metrics, including “relevance scores” and “hallucination index,” and provide explicit source citation from the library within a single interface to assess contextual support for generated answers. MyGPT offers a cost-effective, modular, open-source alternative to commercial LLM services and democratizes knowledge-seeking across multiple domains, including use at remote facilities without internet access.

signals.excerpt:
# Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 1

 Oct 23, 2026 

 By Jian Hu and Lin Chai 

 AI-Generated Summary 

- NVIDIA TensorRT builds inference engines by making interdependent scheduling decisions across graph transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization.
- A mathematical framework models compilation as a builder algorithm generating candidate solutions and a searching algorithm selecting the fastest feasible one under accuracy constraints.
- The Global Performance Tuner, released in TensorRT 11.1, introduces customizable build routes that expand the solution space and validate each candidate against end-to-end accuracy and performance.
- Three principles guide the tuner: accuracy-aware tuning, customizable build routes, and a large solution space from which the fastest acceptable engine is selected.

...

Deploying a trained neural network involves more than translating each operator into a GPU kernel. It is a compilation problem with many legitimate answers. For example, when NVIDIA TensorRT builds an engine, it makes interdependent decisions about graph-IR transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization. This process is called scheduling. Different scheduling choices can preserve model semantics yet produce very different inference performance, making scheduling central to deep learning compiler optimization.

No single scheduling strategy is best for every model and deployment environment. A transformation that accelerates one network may slow another. A kernel that is faster in isolation may interact poorly with fusion, tensor layouts, or memory traffic elsewhere in the graph. Aggressive scheduling may improve performance while violating an application’s accuracy requirement. These coupled, model-dependent effects often appear only after the complete engine is built and measured, making the right strategy increasingly difficult to predict.

This post is Part 1 of a two-part series that is intended to develop a clearer way of reasoning about performance optimization. It explores questions such as: What makes one compiled engine better than another? Why can individually promising decisions fail end to end? How should accuracy constrain performance optimization? It introduces the Global Performance Tuner, a feature for automatic performance tuning released in TensorRT 11.1, and explores these questions through an intuitive example and mathematical framework.

...

The Global Performance Tuner begins with the idea of customizable build routes. For each candidate solution, it validates the outputs against the specified accuracy criterion and measures end-to-end inference performance. Among all solutions that meet accuracy requirements, the searching algorithm selects the minimum-runtime feasible solution from the expanded solution set.

The following three principles define the framework:

- Accuracy-aware tuning: Use end-to-end accuracy as a constraint that guides performance tuning.
- Customizable build route: Make build routes customizable so that scheduling can adapt to each model and deployment environment.
- Large solution space: Construct a rich feasible solution set, then select the fastest candidate whose numerical difference remains within the specified tolerance.

signals.title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last | MIT Technology Review
signals.excerpt:
### Engineer the system, not the model

Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency.

Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance.

GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model's weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive.

The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize. Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat.

# The science behind TorchNeuron, Amazon’s new PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium chips 

## Runtime optimizations and a thorough evaluation process driven by agentic AI help ensure that models written in PyTorch will execute efficiently and reliably on Trainium systems.

 By Robert Hundt, Arash Jamalian, Apoorv Gupta, Charan Shettyhalli Guruswamy, Abigail Fernandes, Rui Silva, Adarsh Singh, Sarang Ozarde , Khaled ElGalaind, Maen Suleiman

 October 22, 2026 

 Key takeaways 

- TorchNeuron, Amazon's open-source PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, used AI agents to narrow hundreds of thousands of Hugging Face models down to 841 representative models for tuning and benchmarking
- Caching and shared-compilation optimizations cut time to the first training step by about a third on a large language model shared across accelerators
- Its opt-in "adaptive eager" mode overlaps compile time with execution to approach fully compiled performance without the overhead

...

This week, we announced the availability of TorchNeuron, an open-source backend that translates PyTorch code into operations executable on AWS Trainium systems. PyTorch code that already runs on other accelerators will run on Trainium with minimal or no code changes.

TorchNeuron bridges PyTorch and Trainium, and both sides gain from it. PyTorch developers can now run their code on Trainium, which was built from the ground up for large-tensor workloads. They can also tap the AWS Neuron SDK, which includes a profiler that traces each instruction with cycle-level accuracy and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI, pronounced "Nikki"), which enables control almost at the assembly level.

TorchNeuron enables seamless integration between PyTorch models, the AWS Neuron SDK, and AWS Trainium chips.

TorchNeuron includes several optimizations that enable PyTorch code to run efficiently on Trainium, including caching at multiple levels and an optional “adaptive eager” mode that doesn’t execute individual operations one by one, as is typical in plain eager mode, but instead groups and compiles operations for more efficient execution, approaching fully compiled performance.

...

Much of the innovation behind TorchNeuron, however, is the way its performance was evaluated. AI agents searched through hundreds of thousands of open-source models and categorized them according to their architectural characteristics. This allowed the Annapurna team around Khaled ElGalaind and Sarang Ozarde to identify 841 representative models covering the full spectrum of model architectures. From those models, they also distilled tens of thousands of practically important tensor dimensions, or “shapes”, which were then used to tune and benchmark TorchNeuron’s performance. The result is that PyTorch programmers can trust TorchNeuron to execute their code accurately, efficiently, and most importantly, right out of the box.

...

In a distributed training setup, caching also leverages all processes participating in the run. Processes that run the same part of the model need the same NEFFs, so on a single machine, dozens of them may ask for identical compiled code. TorchNeuron runs a shared compilation service so that each operation is compiled only once per machine, and the other processes reuse the result, without overwhelming the host CPUs. In tests with a large language model spread across 64 processes on a single machine, the service cut the time to the first training step by about a third.

...

All this testing and the wide coverage of models give us confidence that TorchNeuron will execute PyTorch models accurately and efficiently on Trainium, giving our customers more options as they confront an increasingly crowded AI landscape.

Posted on Oct 23 • Originally published at hostingpodium.com
# vLLM & TGI Tensor Parallelism: Scaling Quantized Open-Weight LLMs on Multi-GPU Nodes
*> Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.
*
**> Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics:
**> Test your stack live with our
**> Rich Snippets Generator & Schema.org JSON-LD Creator
**> ,
**> Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker

**> 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools

This guide explains how to serve quantized open-weight LLMs at enterprise scale using vLLM and TGI with tensor parallelism and paged-attention KV cache on multi-GPU nodes.
## Executive Overview
This guide details a production-grade pipeline for serving quantized open-weight large language models (LLMs) using vLLM and Text Generation Inference (TGI) on nodes equipped with eight or more NVIDIA H100 GPUs. It covers tensor-parallel execution, paged-attention KV cache, AWQ/GPTQ/FP8 quantization paths, and the observability stack required to meet sub-100 ms private inference latency at 150 TPS.
## System Context
Enterprises typically isolate LLM inference behind a zero-trust VPC, expose a gRPC endpoint, and enforce per-tenant rate limits. The compute plane consists of a Linux host (RHEL 9.4) with kernel 5.14, CUDA 12.4, and NCCL 2.20. The storage plane holds model checkpoints on a high-throughput NVMe RAID10 (3 TB/s read) mounted at `/mnt/models`. All components run as systemd services inside a non-root user namespace to reduce attack surface.
## Tensor Parallelism in vLLM
vLLM implements tensor parallelism by sharding each transformer layer’s weight matrices across `world\_size` GPUs. The sharding granularity is controlled by the environment variable `VLLM\_TENSOR\_PARALLEL\_SIZE`. For an 80-B parameter model on eight H100s, a size of 8 yields a per-GPU weight footprint of \~10 GB, fitting comfortably in HBM2e.
```
# Example launch on a single node with 8 GPUs
export VLLM_TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE=8
export VLLM_DISABLE_LOGGING=1
python -m vllm.entrypoint \
    --model /mnt/models/llama-80b \
    --tensor-parallel-size $VLLM_TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE \
    --port 8080 \
    --max-num-batched-tokens 8192
```
Key parameters:
* **max\_num\_batched\_tokens**: caps the total token count across all concurrent requests; set to 8192 for 8-GPU nodes to keep GPU memory under 90 %.
* **gpu\_memory\_utilization**: vLLM defaults to 0.90; lowering to 0.85 forces earlier KV eviction, reducing tail latency at the cost of throughput.
## PagedAttention KV Cache Optimization
PagedAttention replaces a monolithic KV cache with a per-token page table, allowing the cache to spill to host RAM when GPU memory is exhausted. The page size is 64 KB, aligned to HBM page boundaries. Enabling it requires the flag `--enable-paged-attention` and the kernel parameter `vm.max\_map\_count=262144` on the host.
```
# sysctl tuning for PagedAttention
sudo sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=262144
sudo sysctl -w vm.swappiness=1
```
Performance impact measured on a synthetic benchmark (prompt length 128, generation length 32) shows a 12 % reduction in peak GPU memory usage and a 4 % increase in throughput when the cache exceeds 2 GB per GPU.
## Quantization Paths: AWQ, GPTQ, and FP8
Quantization reduces memory bandwidth and improves arithmetic intensity. The guide evaluates three pipelines:
|Method|Bit-width|Weight-only / Activation|Observed Throughput (tokens/s)|Latency (ms)|
|AWQ|4-bit|Weight-only|2100|38|
|GPTQ|3-bit|Weight-only|1900|42|
|FP8|8-bit (E4M3)|Weight + Activation|2400|34|
FP8 delivers the highest raw throughput but requires NVIDIA's `--fp8-enabled` flag and a driver version ≥ 550.0. AWQ and GPTQ are compatible with older drivers and provide comparable accuracy for instruction-following tasks.
```
# Convert a HuggingFace checkpoint to AWQ 4-bit
python -m awq.convert \
    --model-dir /mnt/models/llama-80b \
    --output-dir /mnt/models/llama-80b-awq4 \
    --bits 4 \
    --group-size 128
```
## Multi-GPU Deployment Walkthrough
The following steps assume a Kubernetes cluster with GPU device plugins. A custom Helm chart deploys vLLM and TGI side-by-side, each exposing a separate service.
```
# values.yaml excerpt for vLLM
replicaCount: 1
image:
  repository: hostingpodium/vllm
  tag: 0.4.2
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 8
  requests:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 8
environment:
  - name: VLLM_TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE
    value: "8"
  - name: VLLM_ENABLE_PAGED_ATTENTION
    value: "1"
  - name: VLLM_MAX_NUM_BATCHED_TOKENS
    value: "8192"
```
For TGI, the chart sets `--max-batch-prefill-tokens=4096` and `--max-batch-total-tokens=16384`. Both services share the same model directory via a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) with `ReadWriteMany` access.
## Kernel Parameter Tuning
High-throughput inference stresses the Linux scheduler and NIC buffers. The following sysctl adjustments are recommended on each node:
```
# Network buffers
net.core.rmem_max = 134217728
net.core.wmem_max = 134217728
net.core.somaxconn = 4096
# Scheduler
kernel.sched_min_granularity_ns = 1000000
kernel.sched_wakeup_granularity_ns = 1500000
# Transparent Huge Pages
vm.nr_hugepages = 10240
```
After applying, verify with `sysctl -a | grep -E "net.core|kernel.sched|vm.nr\_hugepages"`.
## Observability Stack
Metrics are emitted via OpenTelemetry and scraped by Prometheus. Key series include:
* `vllm\_gpu\_memory\_bytes{gpu="0"}`
* `tgi\_request\_latency\_seconds\_bucket`
* `kv\_cache\_page\_evictions\_total`
Grafana dashboards plot 95th-percentile latency against request concurrency. Alerts trigger when `vllm\_gpu\_memory\_bytes` exceeds 95 % of `nvidia\_smi\_memory\_total\_bytes` for more than 30 s.
## Runbook: Latency Spike Diagnosis
* Confirm GPU utilization with `nvidia-smi dmon -s u`. If > 95 %, consider lowering `VLLM\_MAX\_NUM\_BATCHED\_TOKENS` or increasing `gpu\_memory\_utilization` threshold.
* Check KV cache eviction rate: `curl http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=kv\_cache\_page\_evictions\_total`. A sudden rise indicates the cache is thrashing.
* Inspect network queues: `ss -s` and `tc -s qdisc show dev eth0`. Queue drops > 0 suggest NIC buffer saturation.
* If the issue persists, restart the vLLM pod with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/vllm` and monitor for regression.
## Architectural Trade-offs
Choosing between weight-only and weight + activation quantization hinges on latency versus accuracy. FP8 halves the activation bandwidth but introduces a 0.2 % BLEU drop on translation benchmarks. AWQ retains baseline accuracy but consumes an additional 0.8 GB of GPU memory per model due to group-wise scaling factors.
Tensor parallelism scales linearly up to the point where NCCL collective overhead dominates. Empirical measurements on eight H100s show a 7.2× speedup over single-GPU baseline; adding a second node (16 GPUs total) yields only a 12.5× gain because inter-node PCIe latency adds \~0.6 ms per attention head.
## Security Hardening
All inference pods run with `runAsNonRoot:true` and `readOnlyRootFilesystem:true`. Model files are stored on an encrypted LUKS volume mounted at `/mnt/models`. Access to the gRPC endpoint is limited to a mutual-TLS mesh using SPIFFE identities. Audit logs capture every request ID, tenant, and model version.
## Future Extensions
Integrating NVIDIA's MPO (model parallelism optimizer) can reduce NCCL traffic by merging all-reduce calls across layers. Additionally, migrating the KV cache to NVMe-based persistent memory (PMEM) would allow cache sizes > 64 GB without sacrificing latency, provided the page-fault path is tuned with `numactl --interleave=all`.

by Anthony Liguori, James Ward, and Libby Clark on 22 OCT 2026 in Open Source Permalink Share

The API format that a growing number of model providers use to call language models now has a vendor-neutral home. Open Responses has joined the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) as a project, bringing it under open governance alongside MCP and A2A.

Based on the OpenAI Open Responses API, Open Responses is an open source specification that defines a single API format for calling language models, streaming results, and orchestrating tool use. Build your agent against an open API format and keep the freedom to evaluate new models, switch providers, or run multi-provider setups without reworking your application logic.

AWS is involved in Open Responses and employs a core maintainer on the project, and Amazon Bedrock already supports the Responses API across dozens of models. You can start building today against an API format that’s on a path to becoming an industry standard.

...

Developers building agentic applications face a fragmented landscape of model APIs. OpenAI pioneered the Responses API for stateful conversations that call external tools or functions. Anthropic developed its own Messages API with different conventions for tool use and streaming. Google’s Gemini API takes yet another approach.

Each encodes similar primitives including messages, function calls, tool usage, and multimodal inputs but does so differently enough that your orchestration code is tied to whichever provider you started with. Open Responses standardizes these concepts into a shared specification with versioning, compliance tests, and extensibility rules, that defines:

- A common request/response model — one schema for structured inputs and outputs that works across OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, local models, and any provider that implements the spec.

- Items as the atomic unit of context — a clear schema for messages, tool invocations, and reasoning state, with defined state machines (in_progress, completed, failed) for predictable behavior.
- Semantic streaming events — meaningful event types like response.output_text.delta and response.completed rather than raw text deltas, so clients can be built once and work across providers.
- Extensibility without fragmentation — provider-specific tools and item types are namespaced with provider slugs, keeping the portable core clean while preserving room for innovation.

Practically, this means you pick a model provider based on which model is best for the job, not which SDK you’ve already committed to. # PACE 4-Bit State Quantizer Matches 8-Bit DAMP at 2/3 Memory 

 By Alexis Dufresne · Published October 22, 2026 at 09:40 UTC · Updated October 22, 2026 at 09:45 UTC 

## TL;DR

- PACE rounds the recurrent state once every eight generated tokens instead of after every token, holding the tokens in between in a small decode buffer.
- On four Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 hybrids from 4B to 35B, PACE-4/8 is competitive with eight-bit DAMP on the three larger models at about two thirds its memory.
- PACE-4, with all heads at four bits, scores higher than Q-Mamba at equal memory and needs no fine-tuning.

A new post-hoc quantizer rounds the recurrent state of linear-attention language models to four bits by rounding it less often: once every eight generated tokens instead of after every token, which is where prior four-bit methods lost accuracy. The method is called PACE, and the paper went up on Hugging Face on 22 October.

The setup matters because at 64 concurrent sequences 'the fp32 states take between 10 and 41 % of the memory that weights and states occupy together,' and shaving that lets more sequences share an accelerator. Prior four-bit quantizers either fine-tune part of the weights or lose accuracy; the eight-bit alternative, DAMP, 'reports 9.9 bits per value' and leaves memory on the table.

...

On four hybrid backbones, Qwen3.5-4B, 9B, 27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, PACE-4/8 is 'competitive with eight-bit DAMP on the three larger models at about two thirds of its memory,' and 'PACE with four-bit heads throughout scores higher than Q-Mamba at equal memory.' On the smallest 4B backbone its average is lower than DAMP INT8, with 'lower scores on GSM8K, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.' None of the structure PACE relies on 'is shown to carry over to other model families, to models whose layers are all recurrent, or to token mixers with a different update or decay.' Throughput was measured only on Qwen3.5-4B on one H100 PCIe GPU at a 512-token context, with Triton kernels released for periodic decoding over a packed four-bit state. It arrives in the middle of a busy week for inference research on our tracker.

...

If your inference stack serves Qwen3.5 or Qwen3.6 hybrids at batch, PACE is a drop-in way to cut recurrent-state memory by roughly a third without retraining; it is not shown to transfer to other model families, so treat the win as backbone-specific for now.

Agents spend much of their time waiting on tools. A coding agent may start a build that runs for twenty minutes, a triage agent may wait hours for the next pull request on a repository, and an assistant may wait until the next morning for an approval. A 1.2-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts configuration, 58.36 billion active parameters per token, 512 NVIDIA B300 GPUs, and a measured peak of 858 TFLOP/s per accelerator. Those are the headline numbers from Ai2's OLMo-Core 3, the latest iteration of the Allen Institute for AI's open training infrastructure. But the number that matters most is buried in the methodology: the trillion-parameter tests used random routing. No learned expert selection, no converged language model, no downstream benchmark scores. OLMo-Core 3 is not a model. It is the machinery for building one, released as an inspectable, forkable training stack. That distinction, easily missed in a landscape obsessed with parameter counts, is precisely what makes this release significant. Tianhua Tao and collaborators at Ai2 and the University of Washington have published the work under the title 'Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training.'

...

The throughput advantage is concrete but narrow in scope. On a 47-billion-parameter MoE test, OLMo-Core 3 delivered approximately 2.7 times the throughput of OLMo-Core 2, the previous iteration. Ai2 also reports a 21 percent throughput improvement and reduced peak active memory when using MXFP8 precision for suitable operations relative to BF16. However, neither result comes with the full set of controls needed for cross-system comparison: sequence length, batch size, number of experts, top-k routing configuration, communication topology, duration, and whether the measurement captures steady-state microbenchmark performance or end-to-end training including checkpointing, evaluation, data loading, and failure recovery. The 858 TFLOP/s figure, multiplied across 512 GPUs, implies roughly 439 PFLOP/s of aggregate observed throughput. Whether that number uses a dense-equivalent FLOP convention, counts only physically executed operations, or includes communication idle time remains unspecified in available documentation.

...

What most coverage will get wrong is threefold. First, OLMo-Core 3 will be described as 'an open trillion-parameter AI model.' It is not. No evidence exists that a trained 1.2T-parameter language model was produced, evaluated, or released. The trillion-parameter configuration is a systems benchmark, not a capability demonstration. Second, 858 TFLOP/s per GPU will be treated as an efficiency metric comparable across systems. It is not, without matching GPU generation, precision format, sequence length, batch size, expert count, routing policy, communication overhead, and measurement methodology. Third, the 2.7x throughput improvement will be interpreted as a 2.7x reduction in training cost. Throughput and cost diverge whenever communication, checkpointing, failure recovery, data loading, and routing instability consume non-trivial fractions of wall-clock time. Random routing, by definition, avoids the load imbalance and expert collapse that make real MoE training difficult.

# Liquid AI Launches RIPL, a Real-Time Inference Engine for Sub-50 ms LFMs

By

Asif Razzaq

October 22, 2026

Liquid AI just announced Liquid RIPL, short for Real-time Inference Pipeline. RIPL is a low-latency engine that serves Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) inside a live request path. It returns complete generated responses end-to-end in under 50 ms. It also claims that latency holds while traffic arrives continuously at peak load. For developers, the message is simple. Swap gradient-boosted trees for a generative model, and keep the latency budget.

## TL;DR

- Engine: Serves LFM2.5 models from 230M to 2.6B parameters
- Runs on: Enterprise deployments on NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Benchmarks used a single B200.
- Performance: 5.6 to 28.4x lower p95 latency than Qwen3.5 on vLLM, per Liquid’s own tests.
- Best: LFM2.5-1.2B hit 155.8 ms p95 vs 4,431 ms for Qwen3.5-0.8B, a 28.4x gap (256 in, 128 out).
- Worst: LFM2.5-2.6B gained only 5.6x (449.1 ms vs 2,499 ms). Sub-50 ms fails on longer requests.

...

## RIPL benchmarks: how fast is it vs vLLM?

Liquid measured p95 end-to-end latency under open-loop Poisson arrivals on one B200. LFMs ran on RIPL. Baselines, including MiniCPM5 and Granite 4.2, ran on vLLM.

| Workload | Load | LFM2.5 on RIPL (p95) | Qwen3.5 on vLLM (p95) | Gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1B class, 32 in → 32 out | 1,000 req/s | 34.6 ms (1.2B) | 498 ms (0.8B) | 14.4x |
| 1B class, 256 in → 128 out | 400 req/s | 155.8 ms (1.2B) | 4,431 ms (0.8B) | 28.4x |
| 2B class, 32 in → 32 out | 1,000 req/s | 76.4 ms (2.6B) | 586.8 ms (2B) | 7.7x |
| 2B class, 256 in → 128 out | 300 req/s | 449.1 ms (2.6B) | 2,499 ms (2B) | 5.6x |

Source: Liquid AI blog, Figure 2. Sealf-reported.

Liquid AI also mapped 6 real-time workloads against fixed budgets:

- Adtech query rewriting: 32 in, 32 out, 50 ms budget, LFM2.5-350M.
- Search intent classification: 128 in, 1 out, 20 ms budget.
- Search reranking: 1k in, 1 out, 30 ms budget.
- Payments risk scoring: 512 in, 16 out, 50 ms budget, LFM2.5-1.2B.
- Credit decisioning: 8k in, 64 out, 150 ms budget.
- Image alt text: 512×512 image and 64 tokens in, 16 out, 100 ms budget, LFM2.5-VL-450M.

signals.title: Remember everything, read only what matters: why financial AI agents need a context layer: By Jan Daniel Semrau
signals.excerpt:
Ternary Capital launches deepcq.com, the home of DeepCQ, an open-source neurosymbolic context layer that cuts agent input tokens by more than half while making every model input deterministic and explainable.

Financial institutions are moving from chatbots to agents: systems that run for hours or days, call tools, accumulate notes and work through multi-step research and operations tasks. That shift exposes a problem few budgets anticipated. Most agent pipelines resend their entire memory to the model on every call.

...

Introducing DeepCQ

Today Ternary Capital, the world's leading cognitive financial agents lab, is launching deepcq.com, the home of DeepCQ (Deep Context Query).

DeepCQ sits just before prompt assembly. It organises an agent's memory into five tiers, modeled on how the human brain separates live state, working memory, recent conversation, long-term knowledge and static reference data, each with its own lifetime and update rule. Before every model call, it scores each memory section against the question and passes on only the sections that matter, along with a record of why.

Results from production

Evaluated on 1,000 production queries from a multi-turn investment-research agent against a full-context baseline, DeepCQ delivered:

- 57.6% fewer input tokens on average, ranging from 40% to 70% depending on query type 
- A 0.6-point gain in answer relevance on a 5-point human rating (3.9 to 4.5), with correctness and completeness held or improved 
- A false-negative rate of 0.8%, meaning needed context was rarely left out 
- Duplicate tool calls cut from 18% to under 1% 

The research behind DeepCQ has been accepted at ICTIR 2026, the ACM SIGIR International Conference on the Theory of Information Retrieval. Read the paper (PDF).

...

For regulated institutions, the more important property may not be the savings but the auditability. DeepCQ has no model in the selection loop. The same question over the same memory always produces the same context. Every result lists which sections were included, which were excluded, their scores and the exact terms that matched.

That means what reaches the model can be reviewed, unit-tested and kept under version control, the same way banks already govern other production logic. When nothing matches, DeepCQ fails open: it sends the full context rather than a silently truncated prompt, and records that it did so, so fallbacks can be monitored and counted. For model risk, compliance and internal audit teams being asked to sign off on agentic systems, a deterministic, explainable record of model inputs is a meaningful step forward.

Complementary to RAG, not a replacement

DeepCQ is pure Python with zero dependencies and no embedding stack. It works in front of any model and alongside existing retrieval pipelines: RAG decides which documents to fetch, DeepCQ decides what actually reaches the prompt. Examples are available for the OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, Qwen and Google A2A.

Open source and available today

DeepCQ is released under the MIT license on GitHub and installs from PyPI with a single command: `pip install deepcq`. At deepcq.com, readers can run the algorithm live in the browser, explore the benchmarks and read the paper.

Today, we’re excited to release Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB — our latest open small language model optimized for speed and intelligence per GB in conversational agents.

Bolt E4B builds on Gemma 4 E4B with Nemotron post-training. It combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on NVIDIA GeForce RTX, Jetson, RTX Spark and DGX Spark.

Bolt E4B offers ~40% higher average quality against our prior model on key conversational agent benchmarks and outputs up to ~80% fewer tokens vs peers.

Designed to pack conversational agent intelligence into as little as ~4GB in its target workloads, Bolt E4B enables responsive local experiences while preserving headroom for applications and other models in the same pipeline.

...

After post-training, we quantized the selected BF16 checkpoint to Q4_K_M using llama.cpp with importance-matrix (imatrix) calibration. Calibration used approximately 1M tokens of RL rollouts from the same training step as the selected checkpoint.
